title: The Network Edge, the Network Core, and Packet Switching
summary: The Internet as two parts — end systems at the edge running applications, and a mesh of routers and links in the core moving their data — and packet switching, the core's strategy of chopping messages into small units and forwarding each one independently instead of reserving an end-to-end circuit.

references.label: Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Networking and Communication Knowledge Area

title: Protocol Layering and the Internet Stack
summary: Splitting the impossibly complex job of networking into five layers — application, transport, network, link, physical — each hiding its own machinery behind a fixed service to the layer above, the exact same information-hiding discipline already covered as a software-design principle, now applied to protocol design.

references.label: Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)
Stanford CS144 — Introduction to Computer Networking

title: Delay, Loss, and Throughput in Packet-Switched Networks
summary: Four kinds of delay a packet accumulates at every hop — processing, queuing, transmission, propagation — plus loss from full buffers and throughput as the actual rate data moves, with the bandwidth-delay product giving the real numbers behind why a single slow link anywhere on a path can dominate an entire connection's performance.

references.label: Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Networking and Communication Knowledge Area

title: The Client-Server and P2P Application Architectures
summary: Two structural answers to "who talks to whom": a client-server architecture with an always-on server all clients address, versus a peer-to-peer architecture where intermittently-connected end systems serve each other directly — a real design choice with real scalability tradeoffs, not just a historical curiosity.

references.label: Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)
Stanford CS144 — Introduction to Computer Networking

title: HTTP and the Web
summary: HTTP's request-response cycle, its deliberate statelessness (and cookies as the bolted-on workaround), and persistent versus non-persistent connections — the concrete application-layer protocol every worked example later in this discipline traces down through every lower layer.

references.label: Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)
Stanford CS144 — Lecture Schedule ("Application protocols")

title: DNS: The Internet's Directory Service
summary: A distributed, hierarchical database — root, top-level-domain, and authoritative servers — that translates a human-readable name into the IP address every lower layer actually needs, resolved through a chain of iterative and recursive queries and made fast in practice almost entirely by caching.

references.label: Stanford CS144 — Lecture Schedule ("DNS")
Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)

title: Transport Services: Multiplexing, UDP, and TCP
summary: The transport layer's job is process-to-process delivery on top of the network layer's host-to-host delivery — multiplexing/demultiplexing via port numbers, and a real choice between UDP (bare-minimum, no guarantees) and TCP (reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled), with real applications on each side of that choice.

references.label: Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)
Stanford CS144 — Lecture Schedule ("Transport & reliability")

title: Reliable Data Transfer Principles
summary: Building reliability on top of an unreliable channel from first principles — acknowledgments, sequence numbers, timers, and retransmission — then pipelining multiple in-flight packets for throughput, with Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat as the two real strategies for what a receiver does when packets arrive out of order.

references.label: Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)

title: TCP Segment Structure and the Three-Way Handshake
summary: TCP's real segment header (sequence and acknowledgment numbers, SYN/ACK/FIN flags, window size), and the three-way handshake — SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — that establishes a connection's initial sequence numbers before a single byte of application data moves.

references.label: Stanford CS144 — Lecture Schedule ("TCP & Congestion control")
Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)

title: TCP Reliable Data Transfer in Practice
summary: How the general reliable-data-transfer principles become TCP's actual mechanism: cumulative acknowledgments, fast retransmit on triple duplicate ACKs, and adaptive timeout computed from a running estimate of round-trip time — real formulas, not just the concept of "retransmit if it's late".

references.label: Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)

title: TCP Flow Control: The Sliding Window
summary: Flow control protects a slow receiver from a fast sender — the receiver advertises how much free buffer space it has, and the sender's window shrinks or grows to match, a distinct concern from congestion control (which protects the network, not the receiver) even though both use the word "window".

references.label: Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)

title: TCP Congestion Control: AIMD, Slow Start, and Fairness
summary: TCP treats the network itself as fragile and infers congestion from loss — slow start grows the congestion window exponentially until a loss event, then additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease (AIMD) probes gently and backs off hard, a real cwnd-over-time sawtooth traced across several round trips, and the reason independently-run TCP connections converge toward sharing a bottleneck link fairly.

references.label: Stanford CS144 — Lecture Schedule ("TCP & Congestion control")
Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)

title: The Network Layer: Data Plane vs. Control Plane
summary: Forwarding (the data plane: a router's per-packet, local decision of which outgoing link to use, made in nanoseconds by consulting a table) is a fundamentally different job from routing (the control plane: the network-wide, much slower algorithm that computes what that table should contain) — a distinction every following concept in this cluster depends on keeping straight.

references.label: Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Networking and Communication Knowledge Area

title: IPv4 Addressing and CIDR
summary: A 32-bit address split into a network prefix and a host suffix, with CIDR notation (e.g. 128.11.3.0/24) replacing the old rigid class-based scheme with an arbitrary-length prefix — worked subnetting arithmetic showing exactly how many usable host addresses a given prefix length leaves, and why address space had to be rationed this carefully before IPv6.

references.label: Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)
Stanford CS144 — Lecture Schedule ("IP and Forwarding")

title: Datagram Forwarding and Longest-Prefix Match
summary: A router forwards a packet by finding, among every prefix in its table, the longest one that matches the destination address — worked by hand against a small concrete forwarding table — the rule that lets one entry cover millions of addresses while a more specific entry still takes precedence when it applies.

references.label: Stanford CS144 — Lecture Schedule ("IP and Forwarding")
Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)

title: NAT and Network Address Translation
summary: A NAT router rewrites every outgoing packet's private source address and port into its own single public address and a fresh port, keeping a translation table to route replies back to the right internal host — a pragmatic, widely-deployed fix for address scarcity that also, honestly, breaks the end-to-end principle the Internet was originally designed around.

references.label: Stanford CS144 — Lecture Schedule ("DCCP & NAT")
Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)

title: Routing Algorithms: Link-State vs. Distance-Vector
summary: The two families of routing algorithm are not new graph theory — link-state routing runs Dijkstra's algorithm, already covered in full, over a globally-known topology graph, while distance-vector routing runs the Bellman-Ford algorithm, also already covered, with each router knowing only its neighbors' costs; distance-vector's real, honest weakness is the count-to-infinity problem when a link fails.

references.label: Stanford CS144 — Lecture Schedule ("Routing 1", "Routing 2")
Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)

title: Intra- vs. Inter-Domain Routing: OSPF and BGP
summary: The Internet is not one flat routing domain but thousands of independently-administered autonomous systems — OSPF (link-state) runs the routing algorithm already covered inside one AS, while BGP (path-vector, a policy-driven cousin of distance-vector) glues autonomous systems together at the Internet's actual scale, where routing decisions are as much about business agreements as about shortest paths.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Networking and Communication Knowledge Area
Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)

title: The Link Layer: Framing and Error Detection
summary: One hop below the network layer, the link layer moves a frame across a single physical link — framing marks where one frame ends and the next begins, and a checksum (a cyclic redundancy check, in practice) lets the receiver detect, though not always correct, bit errors introduced by real, noisy physical media.

references.label: Stanford CS144 — Lecture Schedule ("Physical and Link layers")
Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)

title: Multiple Access Protocols and Ethernet
summary: When many hosts share one physical medium, something has to decide who transmits when — CSMA/CD (carrier sense, collision detection, exponential random backoff) is classic Ethernet's answer, and a switch's ability to isolate each link into its own collision domain is the real reason modern switched Ethernet barely needs it anymore.

references.label: Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)
Stanford CS144 — Lecture Schedule ("Physical and Link layers")

title: ARP and Address Resolution
summary: IP addresses route a packet across networks, but a link-layer frame needs the destination's MAC address for this one hop — ARP resolves one into the other by broadcasting a query and caching the answer, and that cache is, mechanically, exactly the hash table already covered: IP address as key, MAC address as value, with a real timeout instead of an eviction policy.

references.label: Kurose & Ross — Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (official companion site)

title: Wireless and Mobile Networking Basics
summary: Wireless breaks a quiet assumption of wired Ethernet — that every node can hear every collision — so CSMA/CA (collision avoidance, not detection) and the hidden-terminal problem replace CSMA/CD, and mobility adds the further question of how a moving host keeps its connections alive as it hands off between access points.

references.label: Stanford CS144 — Lecture Schedule ("Wireless")
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Networking and Communication Knowledge Area

title: Capstone: Tracing One HTTP Request End-to-End
summary: One `GET` request, typed into a browser, walked down through every layer this discipline covered and back up again — DNS resolution, TCP's three-way handshake, HTTP's request/response, IP forwarding hop by hop guided by routing's precomputed tables, ARP resolving the final hop, and framing/error-detection on the wire — naming, at each step, exactly which concept explains it, and closing with an honest scope boundary against `distributed-systems-i`.
